text: You get an array of matchsticks. Each value is the length of one stick. Use all the sticks to make one square. You can't break a stick, but you can join them. Return true if it's possible.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — every stick is used exactly once, and each stick goes into exactly one side. So I'm splitting the sticks into four groups with the same sum. Is that right?
Got it. Are there any constraints on the input size?
There are between one and fifteen sticks, and each length is between one and ten to the eighth.

Okay. Only fifteen sticks, so an exponential search is fine. But the values go up to ten to the eighth, so I can't do a DP over lengths, and I'll need to check overflow later. Quick check on the examples. One, one, two, two, two: the sum is eight, so each side is two — three sides of two, and one plus one. So true. Three, three, three, three, four: the sum is sixteen, so each side is four. The four fills one side, but each three needs a one, and there are none. So false.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. There are two ways to see the search. The side view builds side one as a subset that sums to the target, then side two, and so on. The bucket view walks the sticks one by one, and each stick picks one of four sides. A naive approach would try all four to the n assignments and check the sums at the end. This problem reminds me of partitioning into k equal-sum buckets, with k equal to four. I'll use the bucket view with backtracking, and prune early: never let a side go over the target.

Here's the plan. One: if the total isn't divisible by four, return false; else the target is a quarter, and I sort the sticks descending. Two: for each stick, try the four sides — skip a side if the stick would push it over the target, or if it's the same length as the side to its left. Three: place, recurse, and take it back if that fails. Once every stick is placed, each side is exactly the target: they sum to four targets and none is over. One thing worth flagging — the sort is descending: big sticks have the fewest places to go, so failures show up near the top of the tree. And two sides of the same length give the same state, just swapped, so I only try the first. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The main function sorts descending, checks the total, and starts the search with four empty buckets. One thing worth flagging — the over-target line must be continue, not break, because the buckets are not sorted; a full side can come before an empty one. Take one, one, one, one: the first one fills side zero, the next one overflows it, and a break would never try sides one to three, so it returns false. The same goes for the duplicate line: equal to the left neighbour says nothing about the next side, so a break wrongly fails on six twos, three threes and a seven — and small tests won't catch it.

Let's dry-run the code with three, three, three, three, four. Sorted, the four comes first; the target is four, expected false. The four takes side zero, and the threes take sides one, two and three. The key row is the fifth call: the last three fits nowhere. Then on the way back up, every other try is an empty side next to an empty side, so the duplicate check skips it. Just five calls; without that check, sixty-five. Corner cases: one, one, one, one is true — the case that breaks a break on the over-target line. A total not divisible by four needs zero search calls. Twelve sticks of ten to the eighth is true in thirteen calls.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is four to the n in the worst case, since each stick has up to four choices. In practice the pruning is huge: the hardest random fifteen-stick input took thirty-two thousand one hundred forty-two calls, about a third of a millisecond. Space is linear for the recursion stack, plus the four buckets. Overflow: the worst total is fifteen times ten to the eighth, one point five billion, which is below the int maximum of about two point one billion. And a bucket never passes the target, so a bucket plus one stick stays under half a billion. So int is safe. The total mod four check is just a shortcut: without it, the target rounds down, the sticks can never all fit, and the search still returns false — only slower.
How much do the sort and the duplicate check actually buy you?

I measured it on two hard false cases: the hardest random fifteen-stick input, and twelve sticks of ten to the eighth plus two, one, one. Ascending order is still correct but nine point six and eighty-one times slower. Dropping the duplicate line costs twenty-six and five hundred forty-four times more calls — that's the big win. All variants are still correct; only the speed changes. One thing worth flagging — the check only compares neighbours. Since the buckets aren't sorted, two equal sides can be apart, like nine, six, eight, six, and then side three gets tried even though it equals side one. That's still correct, it only costs speed. Checking against any earlier side saves about three percent, so I'd keep the simple version.
What if you want a guaranteed bound, not just good pruning?

Then I'd use a bitmask DP. The state is the set of used sticks, and I fill the sides one at a time, in order. The value for a mask is how much of the current side is filled, or unreachable. From a reachable mask, I add any unused stick that fits, and take the new length mod the side, so a full side resets to zero and the next stick starts a new side. The answer is whether the full mask reaches zero. That's n times two to the n time and two to the n space — at fifteen sticks, thirty-two thousand seven hundred sixty-eight states. And if the question asks for k sides instead of four, both methods carry over: k buckets in the backtracking, or the same DP with the side as the total over k.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You explained why the over-target line is continue, not break: the buckets aren't sorted, and one, one, one, one shows it. You justified the duplicate check as a symmetry argument and backed it with numbers, while noting the neighbour-only check is correct but not complete. And you checked overflow with real bounds against the int maximum. Good work.
